rules: Everything here is an AI draft (provisional_ai_draft): each counted item passed two blind AI checks that were tested on planted errors, and no person has reviewed it.
A finding counts only in the setting its own quoted lines show; read `setting` before carrying it to another setting.
A question's status is a label from fixed rules over its counted findings; `status_check` says whether that label itself passed its check.
Cite the paper and page from the passage, and read the PDF page before relying on a claim.
notes: The paper has no assumption or limitation records, so hypotheses and limits are taken from added passages. RES-PS-ACCURACY and RES-PSA-ACCURACY quote the same lines as RES-ANOVA-BINARY (p3 L40/42-50): their titles describe descriptive Table 2 differences that the same ANOVA finds not significant. CORE, RES-ANOVA-BINARY, RES-PS-ACCURACY, RES-PSA-ACCURACY and RES-CONFIDENCE are graded EMPIRICAL_PRELIMINARY under the rubric's 'the result is not significant' clause; a reviewer who treats a tested null as the result itself could grade CORE and RES-ANOVA-BINARY EMPIRICAL_SINGLE_SETTING (one task, one judge pool). Table 2's cell values are garbled in the text (columns map to conditions only by order) and are not used. The number of judged questions or judgments is not stated in the lines read; only the F(1,12) degrees of freedom appear. The main text says the 10 highest-performing writers were invited (p2 L110-112), while Appendix A.1 says the 12 writers with the highest scores were hired (p6 L59); cards use the main-text figure. RES-CONFIDENCE's quote starts mid-sentence; its opening (p3 L51-52) is added as a passage. RES-ARG-QUALITY and RES-COUNTER-RESPONSIVE come from the authors' own qualitative annotation of four passages. No record seems mislabelled.

method.description: Professional writers wrote counter-arguments to the existing single-turn arguments of Parrish et al. (2022); selected Upwork judges answered two-option QuALITY questions either reading arguments for both options (PSA) or not (PS, snippets only), giving a first judgment after the initial round and a second after the counter-argument round, under 'simple' and 'encourage abstain' incentives, and a 2 x 2 x 2 repeated-measures ANOVA tested these factors' effect on accuracy.

stated_hypotheses: The questions are hard multiple-choice reading comprehension questions, and judges have only time-limited access to the full passage text (5 minutes per judgment in the main task).
The comparison is with an argument-free baseline; text snippets are shown in both conditions.
Only the top half of pilot judges (16 of 32), chosen by their accuracy after viewing the passage, take part in the main task.
The conclusion is confined to multiple-choice reading comprehension; the authors say debate may still help in other set-ups such as highly technical tasks.

passages.text:
Mirroring the mostly null results from Parrish et al. (2022), we find that counter-arguments do
not improve human crowdworkers’ ability to answer hard multiple-choice reading comprehension
questions with time-limited access to the full passage text, compared to an argument-free baseline.
In fact, when abstaining is only minimally incentivized, human accuracy gets slightly worse when
exposed to (counter-)arguments. In the higher-stakes setting where judges are incentivized to abstain
unless they are very confident, there is no effect of the (counter-)arguments.

Although there are many settings in which debate is useful to humans to answer difficult questions,
this advantage may not translate to reading comprehension tasks. It remains possible that debate
4

may be helpful in other set-ups, such as for highly technical tasks. For multiple-choice reading
comprehension, however, the debate set up is potentially harmful to human accuracy, particularly
when human judges do not have a strong incentive to abstain when they are unsure.

method.description: In a qualitative assessment, four of the authors rated all arguments and counter-arguments for four randomly selected passages, two raters per question, on a 1-10 scale where quality means whether the rater could think of a more convincing or more appropriate argument.

passages.text:
In order to better understand the data that the writers produce, we conduct a qualitative assessment of
all the arguments and counter-arguments written for a randomly-selected set of four passages. Four
of us conduct this rating, with two different raters assigned to each passage, such that each question
is independently rated by two different individuals. We first read the entire passage text, then read
through the questions and their associated arguments, counter-arguments, and text snippets.

We rate the subjective quality of the arguments on a 10-point scale, and the average ratings are in
Table 7. We define subjective quality in terms of whether the person rating it can think of a more
convincing or more appropriate argument that could instead be made. We use this definition of
subjective quality to avoid unfairly biasing our results against the incorrect arguments, which are
already more difficult to construct; this measure gives a sense of whether the writers were making the
best effort they reasonably could, given the constraints of the task. We find that arguments in favor of
a correct answer are slightly higher rated than those in favor of an incorrect answer, and that this gap
is slightly wider for counter-arguments than for the initial arguments.

stated_hypotheses: Quality is defined as whether the rater can think of a more convincing or more appropriate argument, a definition chosen to avoid biasing ratings against incorrect arguments, which are harder to construct.
Only four randomly selected passages are annotated.

passages.text:
The range of possible incorrect arguments that could be made is greater than the range of correct
ones, as there are many ways to be misleading and fewer ways to be factually accurate in this task. So
the difference in ratings could reflect the slightly subjective definition of the rating task—if the rater
would have made a different (counter-)argument, they are likely to give a slightly lower rating to the
writer. We note, however, that this difference is small, and that the two raters are fairly consistent
in their assessments, as the average difference between the two ratings is small (below 2 points on
the 10-point scale). The most important point is that all the arguments and counter-arguments were
consistently rated above 7/10, indicating a reasonably high quality in the writing.
